en: The Ritual Manual for the Altar of the Painted Image of the Great Peacock Vidyārājñī Spoken by the Buddha;
Presented by the Grand Master of the Household, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of Daxingshan Monastery—the Duke of Su, who enjoyed an estate of three thousand households, was invested with purple robes, posthumously granted the rank of Minister of Works, and conferred the title of Great Mirror and the epithet of Great Universal Wisdom—by imperial decree. The Buddha addressed Ānanda:
Whatever calamities and afflictions exist in the world—
weapons, famine, drought, pestilence,
the four hundred and four diseases, as well as grief, distress, and strife.
Furthermore, regarding the eighty-four thousand malevolent spirits who afflict sentient beings,
and those whose pursuit of superior worldly and world-transcending aspirations encounters many obstacles—
all of this is due to craving and ignorance since beginningless time.
Through false discrimination, the afflictions of the three poisons arise;
failing to understand the true nature of reality, one accumulates unwholesome karma,
which brings about these various kinds of calamities.
Ānanda, for this reason, I now further explain the ritual for painting the image and the procedure for establishing the maṇḍala and making offerings,
for those who recite the *Buddhamātṛ Mahāmāyūrī-vidyārājñī-sūtra* and for all sentient beings afflicted by calamities and misfortunes.
If one recites this sutra in accordance with this dharma,
all calamities and misfortunes shall be eliminated,
and all aspirations and desires shall be fulfilled according to one's wishes.
Ānanda, whenever suffering, affliction, or calamity arises— whether it be for a king,
his princes, ministers, queens, or consorts, or for bhikṣus,
bhikṣuṇīs, virtuous men, or virtuous women— [one should recite this].
In order to eliminate calamities,
one should perform this either in a royal palace,
at a preeminent site, in a pure monastery, or in one's own original dwelling.
Purify the ground according to the ritual: dig it to a depth of one cubit,
remove all tiles, rubble, and impurities from within the earth,
fill it with pure soil, and level it firmly.
Fill it with earth that is inherently pure;
if there is excess earth, the ground will be exceptionally sublime.
One should smear and wipe it clean, establish a *maṇḍala*, and construct a square altar measuring five cubits.
The layout consists of three tiers, each four finger-widths high;
it may be executed with colored paintings or with five-colored powders.
In the center of the inner court, draw an eight-petaled lotus flower.
Upon the lotus-womb, one should paint the Bodhisattva Mahāmāyūrī Vidyārājñī,
facing east, white in color,
and wearing light garments of white silk.
Adorned with various ornaments such as crowns, necklaces, earrings, and armlets,
he rides upon a golden peacock king and sits in the full lotus posture atop a white lotus flower.
Alternatively, she may be blue-green in color, seated upon a flower,
abiding in the aspect of compassion, and possessing four arms;
her first right hand holds a blossoming lotus.

The second hand holds both the cause and the fruit; the form of this fruit resembles a watermelon. The first hand on the left side is held at the heart with the palm grasping an auspicious fruit (śrīvatsa) shaped like a peach or apricot. The second hand holds three or five peacock feathers.
Proceeding from the right side of the Buddha-mother and circling clockwise,
draw the seven World-Honored Buddhas upon the surrounding lotus petals.
From the Tathāgata Vipaśyin down to Śākyamuni and the Bodhisattva Maitreya,
all sit with their heads facing outward, each abiding in the posture of meditative concentration,
until reaching the eighth petal in the northwest corner.

Paint the Bodhisattva Maitreya with his left hand holding a *kundikā* (water flask) and his right hand raised with the palm facing outward, making the gesture of granting fearlessness (*abhaya-mudrā*).
Furthermore, outside the lotus petals...
In the four directions of the inner courtyard, paint four pratyekabuddhas,
all depicted in the form of Buddhas with uṣṇīṣas on their heads and abiding in the posture of meditative concentration.
Furthermore, in the four corners, paint the four great śrāvakas.
In the northeast corner, depict Ānanda;
next, in the southeast corner, depict Rāhula;
and next, in the southwest corner, depict Śāriputra.
Next, in the northwest corner, paint Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
All [the figures] wear the *kaṣāya* robe with the right shoulder bared.
These are all in the central court.
Next, in the second enclosure, paint the eight celestial kings (*lokapāla*) along with their retinues.
In the east, paint Śakra, the king of gods,
holding a vajra and surrounded by the hosts of devas.
Next, in the southeast, depict the Fire God (Agni).
His left hand holds a *kamaṇḍalu* and his right hand performs the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya-mudrā*).
He is surrounded by a multitude of ascetic sages (*ṛṣi*) endowed with the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
Next, in the south, paint the Heavenly King Yama holding the banner of Yama,
surrounded by the hosts of spirits from the realm of Yama; next, in the southwest, paint the Rākṣasa King holding a sword.
Surrounded by a host of rākṣasas,
next, in the west, one should paint Varuṇa holding a noose.
Surrounded by a multitude of nāgas,
next, in the northwest, paint the Wind Deity holding a banner and pennant.
Surrounded by a host of vidyādhara sages,
next, in the north, paint Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King,
holding a jeweled staff.
Surrounded by a host of yakṣas,
next, in the northeast, one should paint the god Īśāna,
holding a trident.
Surrounded by hosts of bhūtas and pretas—
all of whom belong to the second enclosure. Next,
the third enclosure begins from the northeast corner.
To the right, draw the twenty-eight great yakṣa generals arranged in a clockwise circle,
each surrounded by hosts of spirits and ghosts;
and also draw the lunar mansions, the planets, and the deities of the twelve zodiac signs.
Next, the outer perimeter of the third courtyard is to be plastered with fragrant clay and strewn with lotus leaves.
Place upon the leaves the offerings of food— namely, milk-rice, curd-rice, cooked rice, fruits, and so forth—
and [consecrate them] all with the mantra of the Vidyārāja Aparājita.
Sprinkle consecrated perfumed water.
Arrange offerings on all four sides and present them with various syrups,
such as granulated sugar, rock honey, pomegranate juice, and honey syrup.
Scatter white flowers upon the altar and place four butter lamps at its four corners.
At each of the four gates, place two pure vessels filled with scented water.
On the eastern side of the altar, install an image of the Buddha-mother Mahāmāyūrī Vidyārājñī.
The method for painting the image is as previously described for the painted mandala;
it is simply that one does not establish the boundary paths.
In the central court, one makes offerings of incense such as agarwood and blended perfumes to the assembly of holy beings.
The celestial hosts of the eastern direction should offer incense by burning white resin (*śrīkhaṇḍa*) as an offering.
The celestial hosts of the southern direction should offer incense by burning purple minerals, mustard seeds, and salt mixed together.
The celestial hosts of the western quarter offer worship by burning agallochum mixed with clarified butter.
The celestial hosts of the northern quarter should offer worship by burning frankincense.
The practitioner of recitation stands on the western side of the mandala.
Spread mats of *máoh* grass to serve as a seat,
or sit upon a low-legged stool;
adorn the scripture table and place it before the altar.
One should make offerings of various fragrant flowers to the scripture scrolls,
arranging them in this manner.
Those who recite and read the scriptures should number three, five, or even up to seven persons.
They shall take turns in succession day and night so that the sound of the sutras does not cease;
the essential requirement is to maintain silence,
with the exception of one person within the group who is well-versed and learned in the teachings.
The mantra master shall direct the taking and giving of offerings and respond accordingly;
he shall perform the ritual, form mudrās, and invoke the worthy sages and saints.
The others should simply recite the sutras with a sincere mind.
It depends solely on the frequency of practice;
one should perform the ritual of repentance through prostrations based on the thirty-seven honored ones with earnest sincerity,
at three or six sessions per day.
At their place of practice, whether for one day, two days, three days, or even up to seven days,
all calamities and misfortunes shall be utterly extinguished,
except in cases where there is a lack of sincere devotion.
The reciter of the sutra may be either a layperson or a monastic.
Each day, they shall bathe to become pure and don fresh, clean robes.
When first beginning, they should face the front of the ritual arena.
With single-minded devotion, prostrate to all the noble assemblies.
First, by means of mudrās and mantras,
invoke all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and celestial hosts according to the instructions.
Having made offerings in accordance with the Dharma,
one should earnestly inform [the deity] of the matters sought,
praying for their compassionate protection and empowerment.
Having universally made extensive great vows for the sake of all sentient beings suffering in hardship,
one then sits in the full lotus posture and anoints the hands with fragrant ointment.
First, form the samaya-mudrā:
with both hands, cross the right over the left externally to form fists, then extend the two middle fingers straight upward so that their tips touch; thus it is accomplished.
Forming the mudrā at the heart, recite the Samaya-mantra seven times. The mantra is:
Oṃ samayas tvam. With this very mudrā, empower the four places of one's own body.
These are the mudrās for the heart, forehead, throat, crown, and the point above the crown.
Next, bind the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Vajrāṅkuśa according to the previous samaya-mudrā.
Bend the two index fingers into hooks and beckon toward oneself.
Recite the mantra seven times without interruption.
The mantra for universally summoning all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, devas, spirits, and the entire assembly of holy beings is as follows:
Oṃ vairocana kuśi ākarṣaya ākarṣaya svāhā. Having formed this mudrā, recite the mantra to perform the invitation.
Summon all the assembly of holy ones; not violating their original vows, they shall all come and assemble.
Next, bind the mudrā of the Vidyārāja Aparājita to establish the boundary of the earth and the boundaries of the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Place the two hands together with the right over the left and interlace the fingers inward;
extend the middle fingers straight upward so that their tips touch one another.
Then, place the mudrā upon the crown of the head and rotate it three times clockwise.
According to the distance desired by one's mind, the boundary is immediately established. Recite the mantra seven times:
*Oṃ hulu hulu caṇḍāli mātaṅgi svāhā*. Next, perform the mudrā for universally making offerings to all worthy sages (*ārya*).
Interlace the fingers with the right hand over the left, joining the palms;
by crossing the ten fingers at their upper joints, the mudrā is formed.
Bind the seal at the heart and recite the mantra seven times, then release the seal above the crown of the head. The mantra is as follows:
*Namo samantabuddhānām* (1) *sarvatha* (2) *khaṃ* (3) *udnaṭe* (4) *sphara hīṃ maḥ* (5) *gagana-kham* (6) *svāhā*. Having bound this mudrā and recited this mantra, [proceed].
One is able to accomplish all manner of vast offerings before each and every Buddha, Bodhisattva, and assembly of noble ones, as well as throughout immeasurable Buddha-fields.
Next, one binds the mudrā of the Mother Mahāmāyūrī Vidyārājñī.
Place the two hands such that the right presses upon the left with the fingers interlaced inwardly;
extend the two thumbs and the two little fingers straight upward so that their tips touch one another, and it is thus formed.
Forming the mudrā at the heart, recite the mantra seven times.
As before, empower the four places with the mudrā; then, releasing the mudrā over the crown of the head, the mantra is:
*Oṃ mayūrakīlaṇṭe svāhā*. Next, holding the incense burner, offer it as an act of veneration and invocation.
The assembly of noble ones is addressed regarding the matter sought.
Having thus invited and made offerings according to the ritual,
one then gives rise to a mind of compassion.
In order to rescue sentient beings from their suffering and hardships,
one should recite this sutra and change the various offerings every day before midday.
One should bind the mudrā of the Vidyārāja Aparājita and recite his root mantra.
With the mudrā at the crown of the head, rotate it once counter-clockwise.
Having briefly released the boundary and exchanged the offerings, [proceed].
Then, as before, one should again perform the invitation and the boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*); thus, according to the instructions, one should make offerings and recite this sutra.
All calamities, droughts, and epidemics [will be averted].
Malevolent spirits, curses, spells, poisonous poisons, calamities, and obstacles—
various sufferings and hardships shall certainly be eliminated.
All prayers and aspirations shall be fulfilled without exception.
I have now fully explained the ritual procedures for the offering of painted images and mandalas.
Should one be unable to prepare such a painted mandala,
or if some urgent disaster should suddenly arrive, [one may proceed otherwise].
According to one's own strength, in a clean place,
smear the ground with cow dung (gomaya) and construct a square altar measuring one cubit,
or according to its appropriate size.
Grind white sandalwood to create a circular maṇḍala.
Within the nine positions, install images of the Buddha,
and erect three or five peacock feathers upon the altar.
At all times, burn incense, scatter flowers, and offer milk-rice, curd, and other such items as offerings to the assembly of noble ones.
With a sincere and single-minded heart, recite and read this sutra—
whether once, three times, or even up to seven times.
Whether for one day or two days,
all calamities and hardships will be entirely eliminated,
and all prayers and aspirations shall be fully realized.
At that time, Ānanda heard the Buddha, the World-Honored One,
expound this Dharma of the Great Peacock King Sūtra for recitation and chanting for the sake of all sentient beings facing suffering and hardship in future ages.
Having received and upheld [this teaching] upon their heads, they paid homage to the Buddha and withdrew.
*The Ritual Manual for the Mandala and Image of the Great Peacock Queen Vidyārājñī*, as Spoken by the Buddha. Volume [ ].
